extracted.intended_audience: researchers, research-integrity officers, science journalists, and the broader scientific community interested in retractions and misconduct
extracted.subtask_description: A news-summary of an Office of Research Integrity (ORI) finding and resulting retractions/sanctions for alleged data fabrication in published neuroscience papers. The page reports ORI's findings, retraction notices, and community commentary on accountability and transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Falsification of data (image manipulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: ORI finds that Respondent falsified Figures 2k, 2l, 3a, 3f, 3h, and 3i in Nature 2001 and Figure 5C(b) in PNAS 2005 by manipulating the images to alter the number and location of positively stained cells in the olfactory bulb and olfactory cortex of mice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete example of misconduct: manipulating image data to change cell counts/locations is treated as falsification. The ORI decision names specific figures and the precise manipulation (altering number and location of positively stained cells) as the basis for finding misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retraction grounds: inability to reproduce and inconsistencies with original data
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors' retraction notices state inability to reproduce reported findings and note 'inconsistencies between several images shown in the paper and the original data' (PNAS) and 'we have been unable to reproduce the reported findings... inconsistencies between some of the figures and data published in the paper and the original data' (Nature).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failed replication combined with discovered inconsistencies between published figures and original/raw data are presented as sufficient grounds for retraction; retraction notices explicitly cite loss of confidence in reported conclusions as the rationale.

rubrics_metrics.name: ORI sanction: supervised research requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Zou agreed to a three-year settlement in which he must be supervised while doing any research with Public Health Service money.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An ORI administrative remedy can require supervised conduct of any future research supported by Public Health Service funds for a fixed term (three years in this case); settlements may specify supervision requirements tied to future funding.

rubrics_metrics.name: ORI investigative process: institutional reports plus ORI oversight review
rubrics_metrics.description: ORI's finding was 'Based on the reports of investigations conducted by Harvard Medical School (HMS) and Fred Hutchinson Cancer Research Center (FHCRC) and additional analysis conducted by ORI in its oversight review, ORI found that Dr. Zhihua Zou... engaged in research misconduct.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ORI routinely relies on institutional investigation reports and supplements them with its own analysis during oversight review; institutional findings feed into federal determinations of misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retraction notices: explanation and apology
rubrics_metrics.description: Retraction notices include explanatory language and apologies such as 'we have therefore lost confidence in the reported conclusions. We regret any adverse consequences that may have resulted from the paper’s publication' and 'We sincerely apologize for any confusion it has caused.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard practice in the examples shown is for notices to state the reason (inability to reproduce / data inconsistencies), to withdraw the claims, and to include an expression of regret or apology to the community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorship/signature dynamics on retractions
rubrics_metrics.description: In the Science 2006 retraction notice cited, the retractor states the lab was unable to reproduce the finding and retracts the report; the notice also notes 'Z.Z. declined to sign this Retraction.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retractions can be issued and publicly noted even if one or more co-authors decline to sign; retraction statements commonly record such dissent or non-signature where it occurs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Replicability as a post-publication integrity check
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple notices and the ORI action emphasize that 'efforts to replicate this work' revealed discrepancies and failure to reproduce key findings, which contributed to retraction and the misconduct finding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post-publication attempts to replicate results are an important evidentiary mechanism for detecting problems; inability to replicate, when coupled with data/figure inconsistencies, can trigger corrections or retractions and investigations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and accurate public CVs as a community expectation
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters assert concerns about incomplete or opaque academic profiles: 'academic staff whose CV is not complete, closed to the public, listing retracted papers without disclosing that they are retracted, outdated pages, etc.' and call for universities to ensure updated and accurate CVs online.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Community norm: researchers and institutions are expected to maintain complete, accurate, and transparent publication records (including disclosure of retractions) online; lack of transparency is framed as exacerbating integrity problems and hampering accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: PI/supervisory accountability as an integrity consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters argue 'It is high time that the PIs (supervisors/ mentors) are also held accountable for failure in their supervisory activities. The system needs a change.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond sanctioning the individual who committed misconduct, community discussion includes holding principal investigators and supervisors accountable for oversight failures; supervisory responsibility is presented as a normative standard for research integrity.
